title: Esther 10:1–3
context: The book closes with a brief notice of King Ahasuerus’s tribute and power and of Mordecai’s greatness, recorded, the narrator says, in the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia (10:2; compare the book of records in 6:1). Mordecai is second to the king, great among the Jews, popular with his people, and remembered for “seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his descendants” (10:3). As throughout the book, God is not named. Both traditions read the ending as shared ground: the story ends with the reversal complete, a faithful leader using power for the good of his people, and God’s care for his people left for readers to discern rather than announced.

verses.text: King Ahasuerus laid a tribute on the land and on the islands of the sea.
verses.arminianNotes: King Ahasuerus lays a tribute on the land and the islands of the sea. Arminian readers note that the book ends with a reminder of the king’s vast power. The empire continues, and the Jews live within it under new circumstances.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the notice as a reminder of the setting in which God’s people live. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a brief historical note that frames Mordecai’s greatness in the verses that follow, with no doctrinal question raised.

verses.text: Aren’t all the acts of his power and of his might, and the full account of the greatness of Mordecai, to which the king advanced him, written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?
verses.arminianNotes: The acts of the king’s power and the account of Mordecai’s greatness are written in the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia. Arminian readers note that the narrator points to official records. Mordecai’s rise is presented as part of public history.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the reference to royal chronicles, which recalls the book of records read to the king in 6:1. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as grounding the story in history and as honoring Mordecai’s place in it.

verses.text: For Mordecai the Jew was next to King Ahasuerus, and great among the Jews and accepted by the multitude of his brothers, seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his descendants.
verses.arminianNotes: Mordecai is second to the king, great among the Jews, and remembered for seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his descendants. Arminian readers note that he uses his power for others’ good, a model of responsible leadership.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a faithful leader whose greatness is measured by his care for his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the final verse as closing the book with the reversal complete, while God, unnamed throughout, is left for readers to discern rather than announced.
